paper_title: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous-research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but are limited by short fixed templates, low executability, and weak traceability, and none has been demonstrated end-to-end in a live computer-vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. Five design choices distinguish it: (i) candidates mutate plugins from a verified-reproduction backbone matched to published baselines; (ii) a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands scores candidates on measured GPU PSNR with verbal-gradient feedback; (iii) a standing falsifier subtracts Elo on failure, integrating stress-test survival into selection; (iv) every reported number is bound to a logged training run, and the run cannot terminate while any claim is unbacked; (v) a seven-category 3DGS taxonomy wraps EVOLVE-BLOCK markers in domain-aligned scaffolds transferable across 3DGS repositories. On PSNR-targeted runs, SplatLab's manuscripts beat their reproduced targets by +0.18 to +3.78 dB, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, for which no prior 3DGS method exists. The research cycle compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute. Code, all manuscripts, experiment ledgers, and the cross-run paper store are available on the project page.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Automating scientific discovery is long-standing research ambition, traceable through early symbolic systems such as the Automated Mathematician [46] and DENDRAL [6], the conceptual programme of AI-generating algorithms [7], and contemporary line of work in which LLMs compose research ideas, write training code, run experiments, and produce manuscripts [25, 48, 35, 11, 24, 41, 9, 37]. The classical research workflow is bounded by an individual researchers time and reading bandwidth, neither of which scales with the publication rate of an active subfield. Automating parts of the cycle could return researcher time to ideation and analysis. Computer vision is natural place to test this: single subfield now produces thousands of follow-up papers in few years, and reproducing one published method often takes engineering effort comparable to producing new one. We are not aware of an autonomous-research pipeline demonstrated end-to-end in computer-vision subfield where reproducing single prior paper takes weeks of expert engineering. Existing systems edit short LaTeX templates over brief training runs, rank free-text hypotheses without executing training loop, or build experimentation on top of LLM-written reimplementations that have not been externally verified against the target paper [25, 48, 11, 24, 35, 41, 9, 53, 20, 17, 22, 45]. PaperBench measures this verification gap: across 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight and Oral papers, the strongest evaluated agent reaches 21.0% average replication [38]. Without verified reimplementation, an improvement claim has no fixed external reference: reported metrics may not trace to measurement on disk, long-running agents drift from their objective as context fills, and comparisons are sometimes made against unspecified baselines. Table 2 summarises four common gaps: domain framework, verified baseline, full-loop refinement, and claim-to-log binding. Progress on this problem appears to require domain-specialised research stack constructed on top of verified reproductions, rather than only improvements in generalist coding ability. Generalist agentic frameworks [31, 13, 47, 50, 43] were designed for software engineering, where every task starts from fresh codebase, not for the iterative refinement atop verified baseline that scientific research typically requires. Four design choices follow: choose single live subfield, build verifiedreproduction backbone for it, expose structured modification space to the ideator, and bind every reported number to logged GPU run. We instantiate this for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [19], an active subfield of neural rendering since 2023. Reproducing 3DGS paper on top of gsplat [52] requires correct densification scheduling, opacity reset, spherical-harmonic activation, and view-dependent appearance, none of which is supplied by the prompt generalist code agent receives; on 30-paper 3DGS reproduction benchmark, current frontier models succeed on roughly 5% of inputs [16]. The verified-reproduction backbone has two parts: NERFIFY [16] converts NeRF papers into Nerfstudio plugins matching expert-written code; SPLATIFY [15] extends the construction to 3DGS through context-free grammar over modular template with nine composable extension hooks. Every candidate that reaches our experimentation phase mutates SPLATIFY plugin already verified to train, and match its target. We present SplatLab, an execution-grounded research system demonstrated in 3D Gaussian Splatting that produces research manuscripts with verified experiments from one-line prompt, target-paper URL, or no input at all, with every reported number traced to logged GPU run. SplatLab orchestrates 36 agents across seven phases (research, ideation, implementation, experimentation, analysis, writing, peer review) without fixed DAG. Five design decisions distinguish SplatLab from prior autonomousresearch and program-search systems; each is detailed in Section 3. (i) Grounded Elo on real GPU PSNR. Idea ranking uses cascade-weighted, grounding-conditional Elo scored on measured PSNR rather than the model-judged proposal scores of AI Co-Scientist [11], with ReEvo-style verbal gradients [51] fed back to the ideator. (ii) In-loop falsifier coupled to selection. standing adversarial falsifier extending AIGS [24] runs in-loop; each failed attack deducts Elo, making stress-test survival selection signal rather than post-hoc check. (iii) Claim-backed verification. Every number that reaches draft is bound to logged experiment, and the run cannot terminate while any claim lacks backing measurement, binding absent from prior pipelines [25, 48]. (iv) Verified-reproduction backbone. Every candidate mutates SPLATIFY plugin already verified against its target, providing fixed reference for every reported gain. (v) Domain-aligned modification space. Seven 3DGS novelty categories wrap EVOLVE-BLOCK markers and the SPLATIFY island tournament [15] in category-aligned scaffolds; cross-codebase auto-mapper places them in arbitrary 3DGS repositories so the diff space coincides with the fields modification space. On Mip-NeRF 360 [3] and LLFF [27], SplatLab produces manuscripts that each beat their reproduced target by +0.18 to +3.78 dB PSNR, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, domain not addressed by prior 3DGS work. The research cycle (read, reproduce, extend, train, ablate, write) compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute, enabling design-space sweeps not feasible at single-researcher pace. SplatLab, all agents, and the code can be found at http://seemandhar.github.io/splatlab.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: End-to-end automated research pipelines. SplatLab sits closest to systems that take goal and emit manuscript. The AI Scientist and v2 produce ML papers via fixed templates and agentic tree search [25, 48]. Agent Laboratory, MLR-Copilot, AI-Researcher, NovelSeek/InternAgent, Dolphin, and CodeScientist organize the literature-to-paper loop with role-specialized agents [35, 22, 41, 29, 53, 17]; CycleResearcher post-trains an LLM on research-review-refine cycle, and AgentRxiv adds shared preprint pool across runs [45, 34]. AIGS adds post-hoc FalsificationAgent, data-to-paper traces claims back to data, Curie embeds rigor through agent control modules, and PaperBench grades replication against author rubrics [24, 14, 20, 38]. All operate over agent-written reimplementations whose match to the target is itself unverified; SplatLab requires every candidate to mutate plugin already verified to compile, train, and reach the targets headline. None condition on (B, L) pair, none fuse falsification with cascade-weighted Elo, and none allow reviewer-spawned re-experimentation rather than only prose edits. Autonomous discovery without manuscript output. second line of work runs the scientific loop but stops short of paper. Googles AI co-scientist uses multi-agent Elo tournament over 203 biomedical goals with wet-lab validation in drug repurposing and antimicrobial resistance [11]. The Virtual Lab designed 92 SARS-CoV-2 nanobodies validated experimentally [39]; Coscientist and ChemCrow connect GPT-4 to wet-lab and computational chemistry tools [5, 26]. ResearchAgent and Si et al. study LLM ideation in isolation, with the latter finding LLM ideas judged more novel but slightly less feasible than expert ideas in 100+ NLP-researcher study [1, 36]. Wei et al. survey the landscape [44]; we sit at their Level-3 full agentic discovery but instantiate it for graphics rather than wet-lab biology. Closest to our tournament is the AI co-scientists Elo loop, but it ranks free-text hypotheses rather than compiled training runs against (B, L) substrate, and updates ratings uniformly rather than scaling by evaluation depth. Evolutionary program search and multi-agent infrastructure. SplatLabs island tournament with EVOLVE-BLOCK markers builds on LLM-driven program evolution. FunSearch pairs an LLM with systematic evaluator on an island-based loop [33]; AlphaEvolve generalizes this to entire codebases via Gemini ensemble [30]. EoH co-evolves natural-language thoughts and code, ReEvo introduces verbal gradients (LLM reflections on why one heuristic beat another, fed back into mutation), Promptbreeder evolves prompts self-referentially, and Mind Evolution scales inference-time compute through genetic search [23, 51, 10, 21]. We adopt verbal gradients from ReEvo but route them into the ideator rather than heuristic mutator, and replace per-individual fitness with cascade-weighted, grounding-conditional Elo so cheap dry-run wins do not dominate ratings of full-train candidates against the verified substrate. MetaGPT, ChatDev, AutoGen, and SWE-agent supply the orchestration primitives we reuse [13, 31, 47, 50], while LLM-as-a-judge, MARG, and AgentReview inform our reviewer-driven re-experimentation but treat review as terminal rather than gate that can demand new substrate experiments [54, 8, 18].

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: SplatLab is system for verified evolutionary research over reproducible substrate. The substrate is 3DGS reproduction backbone (SPLATIFY [15]/NERFIFY [16]) whose plugins match their published 3 Figure 2: Detailed pipeline of SplatLab. Expanding the overview in Figure 1, research intent (or no input) passes through six stages (grounding, Elo-pre-ranked ideation, EVOLVE-BLOCK implementation, cascade-weighted Elo refinement across eight islands, integrity audit, and reviewer-driven manuscript synthesis) run by three-level hierarchy of Professor, PhD Coordinators, and Undergrad Leaf Agents. targets; every extension SplatLab proposes mutates plugin already verified to match its target. This scaffolding separates SplatLab from prior systems that pursue unconstrained autonomous discovery over unverified agent-written code, whose drafts are neither traceable to logs nor reproducible by retraining. The claim is narrower and stronger: SplatLab performs autonomous iterative discovery within live, technically demanding subfield, with every iteration anchored to measured baseline and bound to logged training run. Formally, given research prompt, target-paper URL, or no input at all, SplatLab returns = (Ptex, Ppdf, L, C) = (x; D), where Ptex is the LaTeX source, Ppdf the compiled PDF, binds every number in Ptex to training run on disk, and is the codebase that produced those numbers. The fixed context = (R, B, H, G) supplies the 3DGS literature corpus R, the SPLATIFY backbone B, the nine EVOLVE-BLOCK hooks H, and the target conference template G. SplatLab produces both and in the same run against the verified B; its writing stage can re-enter implementation to spawn new training runs. Fig. 2 decomposes into six stages, each acting on the same verified substrate: Grounding instruments measured bottleneck on the matched plugin; Ideation pre-ranks candidate fixes by idea-level Elo; Implementation compiles survivors into EVOLVE-BLOCK mutations of the plugin; Refinement runs cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands with standing falsification, scored on real ns-train PSNR; Audit verifies that every reported number traces back to measurement on the verified substrate; Synthesis writes the manuscript through reviewer-driven loops that may re-enter Stages 34. Stages run under three-level hierarchy (Professor, PhD coordinators, Undergrad leaf agents; 36 total) with no fixed DAG: the master may revisit any earlier stage on falsifier veto, audit failure, or reviewer-spawned ablation. 3.1 SplatLab Stage 1: Grounding. Stage 1 anchors the run in the substrate. Two parallel investigations produce the thesis spine Γ, the only artefact Stages 26 condition on. The first reads the literature: Researcher queries arXiv, Semantic Scholar, and Google Scholar and pulls from persistent cross-run paper store via RAG, with retrievals written back before Stage 1 closes so the corpus grows monotonically across runs. Retrieved PDFs are parsed by MinerU [42] and Limitation Brainstormer crossreferences each papers stated limitations against critiques in later work, emitting L-IDs: deduplicated opacity reset destabilises late refinement, each limitation strings such as L-127: with its supporting citation set. The second reads the substrate: Bottleneck Analyst trains the verified SPLATIFY plugin on representative Mip-NeRF 360 scenes and profiles per-tile loss, PSNR trajectory, memory, and gradient norms; patterns become B-IDs: measurement-anchored strings 4 such as B-04: category it implicates. Γ contains the SPLATIFY reproduction vector V, the L-IDs, and the B-IDs. PSNR plateau at 25.65 dB on garden, each tagged with the EVOLVE-BLOCK Stage 2: Grounded ideation. Stage 2 turns Γ into ranked set of candidates worth running on the substrate, all without running any training. candidate is tuple (mechanism, c, l, b, ˆ), where {1, . . . , 7, open} indexes one of seven 3DGS novelty categories, is the L-ID it claims to address, the B-ID it claims to attack, and ˆ predicted delta on the headline metric. An Ideator generates candidates conditioned on Γ over five iterations; between rounds, Web Scout fires fresh literature searches keyed on the previous rounds L-IDs and B-IDs, so prior art widens monotonically rather than re-sampling from fixed window [36]. Each candidate clears four checks: Precedent (the L-ID/B-ID citation set supports the claim), Novelty (neither restatement of prior work nor parameter-only tweak lacking new signal, state, or mechanism, as screened by the Tweak Trap), Saturation (fewer than logged negatives in the category-mechanism cell), and Orthogonality (not near-duplicate of another admitted candidate); rejection routes back to the Web Scout as Meta-Pivot signal. Survivors enter bracket tournament with initial Elo 1200, judged by an LLM-as-Judge along four axes: novelty against the L-ID citation set, specificity to the B-ID, implementability within the category, and predicted-delta plausibility. Top-quartile uses multi-turn debate; lower tiers use single-turn pairwise comparisons. The output passes into Stage 3 where each candidate becomes real plugin mutation, and into the GPU-grounded tournament in Stage 4. Stage 3: Verified-plugin implementation. Stage 3 mutates the substrate. Each surviving idea becomes code change to SPLATIFY/NERFIFY plugin [15, 16] that already compiles, trains, and matches the targets published headline; the verified-plugin contract attributes downstream gains to the proposed mechanism rather than to silent reimplementation drift. Hook Mapper resolves the abstract category into concrete subset of the nine EVOLVE-BLOCK hooks (densification, regularisation, loss, rendering, pruning, initialisation, scheduling, opacity, harmonics) and places EVOLVE-BLOCK markers around the corresponding regions, following [30] but over verified plugin rather than agent-written code; for = open, cross-codebase auto-mapper locates insertion points that span existing hooks, compose them, or introduce new ones. EVOLVE-BLOCKs are paired code comments that delimit regions agents can modify while preserving the surrounding verified implementation. An Implementer generates the code under three constraints: Citation Graph retrieves L-ID/B-IDanchored papers and their published implementations as reference code; Graph of Thoughts [4] controller structures reasoning into generation, aggregation, and refinement nodes so failed branch can be revisited rather than restarted; and context-free Grammar of SPLATIFY restricts output to legal hook-level rewrites. Mutations are emitted as structured diffs [30] rather than full rewrites. The diff is applied, the plugin compiled, and 100-iteration smoke test trains on single Mip-NeRF 360 scene; candidate that compiles, finishes the smoke test stably, and instantiates the requested hooks clears the contract. Failures return to the Implementer with the build log as verbal-gradient signal, capped at repair budget before logging to the cross-run store as build-failure negative. Stage 4: Cascade-weighted tournament. Stage 4 makes the substrate the judge. Each candidate is trained and scored on real PSNR; ratings are conditioned on the grounding pair (B, L) (benchmark ID, loss ID), so strength is tracked per evaluation context rather than as scalar leaderboard. Each candidate flows through four stages of increasing rigour: smoke (100-iteration sanity check), probe (full-iteration on one scene), multi-scene (full-iteration on stratified subset), and the full benchmark, which only the champion enters. Stage updates Elo with weight ws {0.2, 0.5, 1.0} from smoke through multi-scene, so smoke win cannot drown out multi-scene loss; without this gating, three-generation eight-island run on Mip-NeRF 360 would exceed multiple GPU-months. For match between candidates and at stage s, R(B,L) R(B,L) + ws (cid:0)Si E(B,L) (cid:1), E(B,L) = 1 R(B,L) 1 + 10(R(B,L) , (1) )/400 with = 32, initial rating 1200, and Si {0, 0.5, 1} from the headline-metric comparison. Each update is paired with an LLM rationale naming the regime, metric delta, and likely causal mechanism; rationales accumulate in Lessons File fed back to the Ideator as verbal gradient [51]. Smoke failures route to Debugger for up to three patches before logging to the Fail Train. Survivors are distributed across eight islands and mutated by five operators selected by multiarmed bandit over per-operator success rates: Refine (local rewrites), Crossover (two-parent mixing), Single-Parent (one-parent mutation), Tweak (hyperparameter perturbation), and Rewrite (full-block regeneration). Per-island Elo distributions form Pareto front over (B, L); promotion requires Pareto improvement, not scalar dominance. standing falsifier attacks every survivor along three axes: edge scenes (OOD trajectories, extreme exposure), sparse-view reduction, and hyperparameter perturbation within published ranges. Each failed attack subtracts δ = 30 Elo, making stress-test survival selection signal rather than post-hoc check; the falsifier holds veto power before manuscript writing. Once champion emerges, the remaining GPU budget splits between chain (sequential variants extending the winner) and orthogonal (independent branches recombining components from nonchampion islands), shifting from chain-heavy to orthogonal-heavy as the champions per-iteration gain saturates. Stage 5: Integrity audit. Stage 5 binds the draft back to the substrate. Six audits run between the Stage 4 champion and the draft; any failure aborts the run as research log. Provenance: contenthash chain links every reported number to its (experiment ID, commit, config) triple. Faithfulness: the Stage 3 rationale is checked against the diff actually applied, catching drift that PaperOrchestra [37] cannot reach by construction. Novelty: the mechanism is re-resolved against Semantic Scholar with query expanded by post-hoc results, catching prior work the Stage 2 Validator missed. Compute match: the headline metric is recomputed under the baselines compute envelope; gains that fail are reclassified as compute-confounded. Cross-codebase port: the winning hook is ported via the Stage 3 auto-mapper to second 3DGS codebase indexed by SPLATIFY; gains that fail are flagged as codebase-specific. Claim check: every numerical or theoretical claim is resolved against the experiment ledger; load-bearing mismatches terminate the run, closing the hallucination failure mode that AI Scientist [25] drafts leave open. Stage 6: Manuscript synthesis. Stage 6 turns substrate-grounded results into manuscript that, when challenged, re-enters the substrate. The (B, L) pair routes the run: new discovery or beating SOTA triggers Mode (manuscript synthesis), otherwise Mode (research log only). Five writers run in parallel: Summary Writer (abstract, introduction), Body Writer (method, experiments; consumes the Stage 4 Lessons File), Related Work (citation floor enforced via the Stage 1 Researcher), Figure Generator (result plots from the ledger), and PaperBanana [55] (conceptual diagrams). VLM Figure Checker audits axis labels, legend completeness, and number-vs-caption agreement; an Ablation Designer reads the EVOLVE-BLOCK diff and emits leave-one-out ablations, Failure Analyst surfaces residual-error heatmaps, and Visual Comparator tiles qualitative renders against the reproduced baseline. Three reviewer agents argue under an Editor (Methodology, Domain, Devils Advocate); the panel extends AgentReview [18] by demanding new training runs, not only prose edits. New experiments can re-enter Stage 4 with the comment as verbal-gradient seed. The loop terminates when no reviewer raises New-Experiment concern.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate two aspects of SplatLab: the research process, through run outcomes, component ablations, failure analysis, and compute costs; and its outputs, through method performance, idea and manuscript quality, and human and multi-agent peer review. Detailed run outcomes and failure cases are reported in the appendix. Experimental Setup. We run SplatLab multiple times: mix of prompted runs (x is target-paper SOTA), single prompt and autonomous runs (x = , the system selects its own target from the literature); per-run mode and target are listed in supp. None of the runs required manual code edits after dispatch. Each runs SPLATIFY plugin or original source code is verified against its targets published headline or, against the paper reported numbers, before SplatLab begins  (Table 1)  . Standard benchmarks are Mip-NeRF 360 [3] (nine unbounded scenes, including flowers and treehill) and LLFF [27]; every 8th image is held out for testing following [2], with all training runs at 30k iterations on NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. We test inter-domain discovery on three out-of-distribution scenes captured for this work and not previously addressed by 3DGS: nebula (astrophotographic), bubble, and diamond. We report PSNR (dB), SSIM, and LPIPS. Our experiments are designed to demonstrate not equalized search budgets, but system capability under end-to-end operation (with long-run autonomy critical challenge that we overcome). Besides scaling, our benefits accrue through the combination of verified reproduction, structured mutation space and grounded evaluation. Reproduction details, the LLM stack, per-run compute budgets, and per-scene breakdowns are in the supplementary. 6 Figure 3: Qualitative comparison against per-regime SOTA. Columns: ground truth with evaluated region boxed (GT), zoomed crop (GT-Crop), the leading published 3DGS method for that rows regime (SOTA, varies per row; see Tab. 1), and the SplatLab-discovered method (Ours). Across 16 runs, SplatLab trained 198 experiment branches, yielding five verified positives, five marginal results with appropriately qualified claims, five non-PSNR contributions, and one recorded failure. The Appendix details selection rejections, training failures, and outcomes by target regime. Compute cost. Runs used 2448-hour wall-clock budget, averaging 113M API tokens across approximately 1,0001,500 LLM calls. GPU consumption ranged from 236 GPU-hours per run, with estimated LLM API costs of $150250. Detailed accounting appears in the Appendix. Generated Methods vs. SOTA. We evaluate SplatLab on multiple targets in two regimes. Three are out-of-distribution scenes (Nebula, Bubble, Diamond) with vanilla 3DGS [19] as the baseline; the remaining eight target published 3DGS methods on Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, where the discovered variant must beat tuned, peer-reviewed reference under the original papers iteration count, scene set, and compute budget. Table 1 pairs each baseline with the SplatLab-discovered method on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS; Figure 3 shows the regime-matched qualitative comparison. The discovered 7 method exceeds its baseline on PSNR in every pairing, with gains from +0.18 to +3.78 dB, the largest on the astrophotographic nebula scene, regime where 3DGS has not previously been applied. Multi-seed Robustness. To evaluate seed sensitivity, we reran GNS-AA with five seeds. GNS achieved 25.95 0.07 dB, while GNS-AA achieved 26.18 0.05 dB, yielding +0.23 0.09 dB compared with the originally reported +0.18 dB. Other generated studies also use three or four seeds. Improvements within the estimated noise floor are reported as marginal rather than verified gains. SplatLab vs. Prior Discovery Systems. Table 2 positions SplatLab against the eight closest autonomous-research and discovery systems on the capability axes of Section 3. SplatLab is the only system that satisfies all five rows anchoring our contributions: verified-reproduction backbone for live subfield, grounding-conditional idea re-ranking, standing falsifier coupled to selection, claim-backed verification, and reviewer panel that can spawn new training runs rather than only prose edits. We evaluate SplatLab at two stages of its pipeline: ideation  (Table 3)  and final manuscript  (Table 4)  . At ideation, twenty Stage 2 candidates are scored against ten PhDstudent ideas and ten recently accepted workshop / conferences ideas under the blind-expert protocol of [36]. At manuscript, three baseline pipelines each produce draft from five human-verified prompts reverse-engineered from SplatLab runs; drafts are scored against the published 3DGS paper for each prompt under the LLM-as-a-Judge paired protocol of [37], verified by graphics-area human reviewers. SplatLab outperforms prior systems by large margins at both stages and scores close to human ground truth at the manuscript level. LLM and Human Peer Review. We review the top five SplatLab-generated papers against five 3DGS papers accepted at CVPR or NeurIPS 2025 under the NeurIPS rubric (Soundness, Presentation, Novelty on 14; overall on 16, 3.5 = borderline). Each paper is scored independently by multiagent reviewer similar to ScholarPeer [12], with separate agents per review axis and chair agent for aggregation, and by graphics-area human reviewer blind to authorship. The multi-agent reviewer slightly favors SplatLab on every axis (3.6 vs. 3.5 overall), consistent with the residual LLM-judge bias toward AI-generated content [54]. The human reviewer reads the comparison differently: published papers score higher on Soundness and Presentation (3.6 and 3.8 vs. 3.2 and 3.0) but lower on Novelty (3.1 vs. 3.5), with the published set landing at clear accept (4.1) and SplatLab at borderline (3.5). (a) AttDis & Friends, (b) NeedleSwap, and (c) AuditSplat, all accepted as posters. Each row shows pages 18 from left to right. Portability and Taxonomy Ablation. Stages 1 and 36 are designed to operate across domains: agents build the literature corpus and codebase profile, select the evaluation metric, implement structured diffs, and run the tournament, audits, and reviewer loop against the target codebase and benchmark. Stage 2 supplies domain-specific ideation grounding; adapting its taxonomy requires expert effort, whose effect on search efficiency we examine below. On the nebula target, taxonomyguided and taxonomy-free runs improved PSNR by +3.78 and +3.45 dB, respectively. Removing the taxonomy increased token consumption from 47.5M to 85.5M (80%). This single-target comparison suggests that domain grounding improves search efficiency, rather than being strictly necessary for execution. Additional runs outside 3DGS with Stage 2 disabled are described in the Appendix.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: SplatLab shows that autonomous research in live computer-vision subfield is achievable when ideation operates atop verified reproductions and every reported claim is bound to logged training run. From one-line prompt or no input at all, SplatLab produces submission-ready 3DGS manuscripts that each beat their reproduced target on PSNR. The research cycle (read, reproduce, extend, train, ablate, write) that today takes graduate student months compresses to days of mostly autonomous compute, and single research cluster running SplatLab sweeps design-space slices that hand-execution would take years to cover. The bottleneck on autonomous research was never model capability; it was the absence of four ingredients: domain framework, verified baseline, iterative full-loop refinement, and binding from claim to measurement. Once those are in place, the discovery rate is set by GPU throughput rather than researcher time. Broader impacts. SplatLab lets small labs participate in live subfields without weeks of reimplementation. tool that compresses months to days can flood peer review designed for human pace. The per-field cost of building verified-reproduction backbone biases capability toward pre-engineered subfields and well-resourced labs. bug in the integrity audit could mask hallucination instead of catching it. We address the third through Stage 5 audits and Mode archival; the first two need community norms. SplatLab may reduce entry-level research opportunities, motivating AI research mentors and educational use of Mode logs to teach hypothesis formation, debugging, and critical evaluation of evidence. We release the system openly, recommend that derivative submissions be labelled and ship their experiment ledger, and discourage volume submissions. SplatLab is research instrument, not paper-mill backend. Limitations and study-resource accounting are discussed in the Appendix.
